explanation: Start with the max heap’s root as a candidate. Repeatedly take the largest candidate and add its children. Every undiscovered descendant is bounded by an ancestor still on the frontier, so the next candidate is the next largest value. No full-array sort is needed.
timeComplexity: O(k log(k + 1)) time. Each of k removals adds at most two children to a frontier of O(k) entries.
spaceComplexity: O(k) auxiliary and output space. The candidate frontier and returned values each have O(k) entries.
attribution: Original C# implementation and explanation authored for EPI Practice from the displayed problem contract.
correctness: Every not-yet-selected node has an ancestor on the candidate frontier whose heap value is at least as large. Thus the largest frontier node is the largest remaining value in the whole heap. Replacing it with its children preserves the frontier property and emits the top k values with multiplicity.
walkthrough: For heap [14,10,12,4,8,6] and k=3, emit 14 and offer 10,12. Emit 12 and offer its child 6. The next largest candidate is 10, giving [14,12,10].
edgeCases: An empty requested selection produces no output.
Duplicate heap values count as separate occurrences.
The input is a max heap; an arbitrary unsorted array does not satisfy the precondition.
